title: How the world can (and can't yet) govern AI
label: 16 September 2026 · Multilateralism & AI
summary: Two experts explain the big governance problems around artificial intelligence (safety, security, standards, equity and preparedness), describe where international cooperation is already working and where it’s stuck, and set out how the UK can use its technical know‑how and diplomatic reach to help build practical, multi‑country solutions without reinventing global institutions.

speakers.label: Sam Daws
speakers.name: Sam Daws
speakers.role: Senior Adviser to the Martin AI Governance Initiative, University of Oxford; founding director of Multilateral AI; former senior civil servant

speakers.label: Isabella Wilkinson
speakers.name: Isabella Wilkinson
speakers.role: Senior Research Fellow, Digital Society Programme, Chatham House; doctoral student on AI security cooperation

glossary.definition: United Nations — the global organisation of states where countries meet and set international rules.
A group of seven wealthy democracies that coordinate on global economic and political issues.
Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development — a club of mainly rich countries that makes policy guidance and standards.
A new European Union law that sets rules for AI safety, transparency and reporting for companies operating in EU countries.
A smaller group of countries working together on a specific issue, instead of everyone in the world.
AI systems that can act on their own, take steps or run routines without a human pushing every button.
A private‑sector led group where big AI firms share safety practices for the most advanced AI systems.
A UK-hosted summit (2023) that brought countries and firms together to talk about AI risk and safety.
Software whose code is shared publicly so others can use or change it.
A group of 20 major economies that coordinate on big global economic and political matters.
A treaty banning biological weapons; it currently has a small secretariat and limited inspection powers.

chapters.title: What multilateral AI governance has to fix
chapters.takeaway: AI governance must cover safety, international security, rules that work across countries, cultural fairness, information integrity, health benefits and environmental costs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We want to know what the key governance issues are that multilateral bodies should focus on. Sam, would you start?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: There are several big ones. Safety — agreeing how to test, evaluate and share risks and respond to serious incidents.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Security — from cyberattacks to AI helping biological threats or military use. Then regulatory interoperability so different countries' rules don't clash.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Also cultural and language diversity so AI reflects people around the world; information integrity for election risks and disinformation; science and health opportunities; and environmental impacts from big data centres.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: I’d group the problems three ways: shared cross‑border risks (malicious use, loss of control, systemic harms like discrimination), a lack of trusted information about AI’s risks, and poor preparedness — we lack a crisis toolbox for AI disruptions.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Put together, these create a gridlock in international action: many talks, little connected implementation across countries and organisations.

chapters.title: Where international work is already happening — and where it’s stuck
chapters.takeaway: There are lots of dialogues — UN, G7, OECD, small groups and industry forums — with useful technical progress, but binding global rules are still missing and politics complicates cooperation.

turns.speaker: Lord Ahmad of Wimbledon
turns.text: We hear of UN, G7, OECD and others. How would you characterise the current state of play across countries and the appetite for international governance?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: It’s a patchwork — many spaces for dialogue but little ‘connective tissue’ to make commitments actually happen. The UN convened 3,000 people recently, but it didn’t produce a binding deal.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: There are successes: better reporting practices for AI incidents, growing transparency norms led by the G7 and OECD, and emerging scientific panels documenting risks.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: There’s a mix: universal UN talks, regional law‑based approaches like the EU AI Act, and lots of minilateral groups — the Bletchley process, G7, OECD joining broader partnerships, and China’s own groupings.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: But three deep problems cut across the whole AI stack: the dual‑use nature (civilian and military), companies protecting commercial secrets, and the technology’s opacity and rapid change.

turns.speaker: Baroness Crawley
turns.text: So are the hardest issues technical, legal, or political? Where in the ‘stack’ is agreement least likely?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: All three matter. Technical standards can make progress. But military use, export controls, secrecy around datasets and model internals, and fast emergent behaviours — especially with agentic AI — make governance harder.

chapters.title: How worried should we be — and about what?
chapters.takeaway: Apocalyptic headlines are unhelpful; the urgent risks are real — loss‑of‑control behaviours, AI‑enabled biological threats, cyber harms — and they need immediate practical measures.

turns.speaker: Lord Grocott
turns.text: Some say AI will wipe out humanity; others warn of ‘killer robots’. Should we be really worried, mildly worried, or is this academic?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Catastrophic language and Cold War arms‑race metaphors are unhelpful. They polarise and can become self‑fulfilling, pushing secrecy rather than cooperation.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Better to avoid catastrophic storytelling and focus on real problems: loss‑of‑control where systems act in unexpected ways, and concrete abuses in military and policing contexts.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: I’m worried but cautiously optimistic. The real scares are bio‑risks and misalignment or loss of control. There’s growing recognition across governments and companies that safety matters.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Why should we be optimistic — what makes AI different from chemical or biological threats where international control has been weak?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: There’s strong economic incentive for companies to keep public trust in AI. That gives leverage. Also, the UK can play a role on bio‑risks because of its life‑sciences expertise and networks — and there are proposals to strengthen the Biological Weapons Convention.

chapters.title: Private companies, the UK’s strengths, and how diplomacy fits in
chapters.takeaway: Private firms are essential partners but must be accountable; the UK’s technical expertise and diplomatic reach are assets — if government teams work together and invest in capacity building and standards.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prashar
turns.text: Does the UK have the capability to shape multilateral AI talks — and is the Government using it well?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Yes — the UK has three strengths: technical institutes (like the AI Security Institute), a diplomatic tradition that can convene (Bletchley was an example), and close partnerships, notably with the US.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: I agree. The UK’s history in science diplomacy shows we can pull together global buy‑in. But Whitehall needs to be joined up — foreign policy and science/tech teams must coordinate better than in the past.

turns.speaker: Lord Bruce of Bennachie
turns.text: We’ve cut aid and diplomatic posts — how should the UK use its overseas diplomatic capacity to help developing countries adopt safe, useful AI?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Think beyond aid money: in‑kind expertise, partnerships with UN agencies, and national capacity building. Many countries can benefit from simpler, local models for health, education and agriculture.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: The UK should use scenario‑based training — tabletop crisis drills with other countries — and push standards work so model testing and supply‑chain security become global norms.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fraser of Craigmaddie
turns.text: But the private sector shapes much of this. How do we make sure the right companies join international standard processes, and that agreements lead to action?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: The private sector must be in the room — you can’t govern frontier tech without it — but relationships must include accountability. Independent, third‑party evaluators who test models before release are a promising idea.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Agreed, and we also need clear attribution in complex supply chains: who’s responsible if an open‑source model is modified and causes harm? We should track agent behaviour and have ways to roll back permissions.

chapters.title: How to move forward: pragmatic steps for the UK and the world
chapters.takeaway: Don't start a brand‑new global agency now; instead bolster existing forums, push technical standards and evaluator networks, use the UK’s G20 and diplomatic reach, and engage China and other partners pragmatically.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blackstone
turns.text: Should we create a new international organisation for AI or use existing ones?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Don’t reinvent the wheel. Strengthen and resource existing networks — for example, the international network of AI safety institutes — and improve how they share info and standardise testing.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: AI spans many areas, so existing UN agencies will each take on parts (health, labour, security). A single new body with enforcement powers would probably only emerge after a very big crisis.

turns.speaker: Lord De Mauley
turns.text: China’s World AI Cooperation Organization — how is it different and what does it mean for Western allies?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: China focuses on sovereignty, local adaptation and diffusion — offering low‑cost full‑stack solutions tuned to local languages and uses. The West should engage but also offer attractive alternatives aligned with democratic values.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: The UK should push interoperability — linking Western, regional and Chinese forums where possible — and use the UN’s 'dialogue of dialogues' role as connective tissue.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Concrete recommendations for the committee: back an independent evaluator ecosystem for model testing, prioritise biosecurity at the multilateral level, align where useful with the EU and stay close to the US on safety, while building regional offers for developing countries.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both — very clear. We’ll take these points back to the Government and press for joined‑up action.
